speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lewis) was in the process of condemning the New Democratic Party for a motion introduced on Friday and then proceeded to introduce what is in effect a closure motion on the debate. That has become the principle trade mark of the Government. Members of the Government say that they want to give the House more authority. They say they want to give committees more authority. Yet every second motion introduced by the Government in the Chamber is a closure motion. In effect, the Hon. Member has now ended debate with his motion.
He asks that the question be now put. Following speeches that will be given on his motion of closure the Conservatives will use their massive majority once again to shove another Bill through the House of Commons. This brings up the question of the accountability of the Government to the people of Canada. Members of the Government are not accountable for anything they do. I cannot think of one single thing for which the Government is accountable to the people of Canada. For the life of me, I cannot see what the value of the House of

Commons is under the present Government. It is muzzling Parliament.
The Government has an agenda upon which it is acting. Sometimes it does not know who makes the decisions. It does not know who it was who ordered the Canadian Embassy and the PMO to sign an agreement with the French. No one knows who ordered the decision to be made. I ask then what is the purpose of the House of Commons under the present Government? No one here can tell me or Canadians what the function of the House of Commons is under the present Government.
In very legitimate terms the House of Commons should be a law-making institution, but certainly not one which just rubber-stamps laws put forward by the Government. The Government has a massive majority and it can move a closure motion whenever it wants. Not one piece of legislation has been originated in the House since the present Government took office. By its own philosophy of the rich get richer and the poor get poorer what the Government has done is gone through a list of legislation that will benefit the powerful in the country. The Bill before us is another example of benefit to the United States truckers and United States carriers of freight. That is all this Bill is about.
What then is the bottom line of the Hon. Member's motion now before the House? We know that the House no longer originates legislation. It does not even talk about legislation. It has no meaning in the legislative process any longer. If it does not do those things then what does it do? It might be said that in Question Period there is some semblance left of making the Government accountable to the people of Canada. But motions of the sort moved by the Hon. Member throw accountability right out the window.
Even during Question Period a Minister is no longer held accountable for his actions. A tradition has developed since this Government took power wherein a Minister does not have to know what went on in his Department or who made a decision in his Department. It is disgusting to anyone who watches and follows the process.
When the Government was elected it promised to bring democracy back into the House of Commons. That was one of the Tory promises set out in the handbook of promises. It was promise number 299. Yet what have members of the Government done? Every second day they introduce closure in order to get their Bills through, Bills which match their philosophy. They refuse to answer questions in the House of Commons. The Parliamentary Secretary has just hammered another nail into the coffin of accountability of the Government to the people of Canada. People are wondering what the function of the House of Commons is. Does it play a recruitment function for future Governments? No, it does not. The turnover in this place is one-third every election. It is no longer a law-making body. So what does it do? It is certainly not accountable to the people of Canada with motions such as the one introduced by the Parliamentary Secretary.
I would now like to deal with why the Government wants this Bill shoved through Parliament. It wants it shoved through Parliament because it opens up, so the Government says, competition in the trucking industry. It says to all truckers in Canada today, "We don't care how much money you spent on your truck and your trucking service, we don't care how much insurance you had to pay, we don't care anything about that, but what we are doing with this Bill is opening up the industry to more competition from the United States".
It is what they call the Freedom to Move philosphy. They are saying let us have freedom to move not only in the private sector, but in the public sector with Crown corporations, with Marine Atlantic, with the ferry boats that go to the different provinces, and with the freight that is moved from one province to another in eastern Canada. Let us allow the carrier to bring up the cost of freight to match his charges. They say to Prince Edward Island or Newfoundland that, "We will jack up the freight charges to pay for the ferry transportation, we will jack up the charges to the people carrying the freight, the truckers, CN, and the people who are driving their cars across to bring it up to a profit-making venture".
If that is done, and when that is accomplished, what is the need of the Crown corporation? What is the need of it, because nobody will be travelling. Obviously, something will have to be done. People will have to start moving, because they certainly cannot afford to live on those islands with the projected increase in freight costs. What will be done with the loss of service along the coastline, with the coastal boat service now having to make money in the Province of Newfoundland, or the bus service that replaced the rail now having to break even across the province? The fact of the matter regarding the bus service is that it has actually been making money to pay for the salaries in Montreal for the past two or three years.
Under this Bill the fittest survive with an influx of competition from the United States. If it was fair competition, it would not be so bad. Where is the competition when gasoline can be purchased for three-quarters or close to half the cost it is on the Canadian side; that is using our oil that the Government has sold cheaper to a United States refinery than to a Canadian refinery? That is the policy of the Government. A United States carrier will start off with cheaper everything. He moves up here and by himself knocks out predatory pricing, and all of the carriers from one end of Canada to the other. That can happen under this Bill.
One wonders who started this Bill. Was it for the free trade negotiators with the United States? Was this another card to remove all the obstacles to all of the trucking companies in the United States so they could move up here and take over the Canadian market? It could be that that is exactly the purpose of this legislation. It is on the free trade table. It is the deregulation of the trucking industry, the rail industry, the airline industry, and of every other industry so that the Americans can take advantage of the market.

That is what the Government has decided to push through Parliament, again using closure and taking away the rights of the Chamber. It must be admitted that at times certain subjects before the House are addressed too thoroughly; sometimes there are too many speakers and the thing goes on and on. But that is the mechanism for the examination of legislation that we have under the Canadian parliamentary system which was borrowed from the British parliamentary system. Bills that drastically affect Canada, that are bad for Canada but for in respect of the Government does not want to face the music in the standing committees, on radio, on television, and in the House day after day, are the Bills that the Government puts through by closure-those are the ones that it shoves through. The Government has been shoving through a lot of Bills, and that means that there have been a lot of Bills that adversely affect Canadians.
With those few words, I am going to conclude my remarks on the motion put forward by the Government. It is typical. I cannot find anything more typical than this motion presently before the House. There is no sense now in talking about Bill C-19. There is no sense going over it. There is no sense going over the clauses, because it all goes out the window. We cannot even talk about what the Canadian Trucking Association has said. It does not matter any more what they told the standing committee, because closure has been introduced. Our time has been limited by this great Government that told us they were going to restore parliamentary democracy. A moment ago, I was looking for that particular promise number 299 in the list of promises that were made. The Government is certainly restoring democracy; it is democracy as they see fit.
The overriding concern and interest of the Canadian Trucking Association, CP Rail, or of the travelling public on an aircraft is that the Government, by an organized and planned initiative, is putting through this Chamber a series of Bills and laws that will mean that the more rural areas of Canada will receive a lesser service than the richer areas of Canada. The philosophy in this country was always that a carrier, whether it was on the road, in the air, or on the ocean, operating under federal and provincial licences had a responsibility to the people who were being served, either with freight or as passengers. The carriers were told that if they were going to go into the big financial markets of central Canada, or of western Canada, or anywhere, then there was a responsibility to serve the less profitable areas. The philosophy was that if you lived in Newfoundland, Ontario, Alberta, or British Columbia, the regulations would be such as to maximize the possibility of equality of service across the country.
We are now seeing a series of Bills that throw this completely and totally out of the window. The Bill presently before the House, on which the Government has imposed closure, will, over a period of time, destroy the trucking industry in this country. Was it great to see deregulation of the aircraft industry with all of those companies competing under deregulation for routes in various parts of this country? Where are some of those companies today, the ones that have not been

taken over by the major carriers into complete monopolies? Those areas today are wondering what happened to the jet service that was there a year ago. Now there are two-propeller aircraft trying to serve the area. Where have they gone as a result of competition?
That is what will happen to the trucking industry. The United States trucking firms will come into the country under this Bill. They will be given treatment preferential to that given Canadian truckers, and they will assume the routes and take over. People will say that this is marvellous, we have all these United States truckers here, but Canadians will be laid off, and Canadian truckers will go bankrupt. That is the price they will have to pay for this competition. The United States truckers will not buy our gas or pay the taxes on the gas that they will have to purchase on the Canadian side of the border.
That is my short contribution to this particular Bill and motion before the House. I would encourage all members to vote against the motion introduced by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader.

Mr. Speaker, now back to the real world. I would like to begin by putting a few remarks on the record concerning safety.
Concern has been expressed that reform of economic regulations will affect trucking safety and that somehow the federal and provincial Governments will slacken in their resolve to protect the safety of highway travellers. Nothing could be further from the truth. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has stated that safety is and will continue to be his first priority. That commitment has been stated in the national transportation policy set out in Clause 3 of Bill C-18 and it has been restated day after day in the operations of the federal and provincial Governments.
As we should all know very well, the provincial Governments already have effective highway safety standards in place. Those standards are vigorously enforced and our highway safety record is very good compared to that of other countries. In ensuring that safe operations continue, our best allies are the truckers. They know that the biggest losers in unsafe operations are the truckers themselves.
Despite the high level of provincial safety regulations currently in place and despite our good record, the federal and provincial Governments are not resting on their laurels. A uniform national safety code for trucks and buses was approved by the federal and provincial Governments in October 1986. This code is a consolidation and an upgrading of the best safety standards in North America. Most of it is already in place in parts or in all of Canada.
Why then are we creating a national safety code? It is because it is something that is long overdue under any regulatory scheme. Under the code, we will be introducing increased uniformity and compatibility into the existing safety regulations for the benefit of the trucking industry and all users of the highways. I think it is important that we in the
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
House should note, without grandstanding and play-acting, that it be clear for all truckers from the East Coast to the West Coast that the Government is very sincere when it talks about safety. We are not reinventing the wheel, nor are we starting from scratch. To even intimate such a thing would be to ignore 30 years of work on the part of the provinces.
There has been some concern expressed by the trucking industry in certain parts of Canada and repeated by Hon. Members opposite that the national safety code will not be completely in place when the new Motor Vehicle Transport Act is implemented on January 1, 1988. Let me inform the House of exactly what is there now and what will be there in the way of highway safety programs and standards for trucks and buses. The following five programs are in place in each and every province: First, driver testing. A driver-licence system which consists of different classes of licences that require periodic testing of truck drivers and filing of medical reports is in existence as well as stringent medical standards for truck drivers and extensive knowledge and skill testing for those who wish to qualify for a driver's licence. Second, driver control. No province allows any driver to hold more than one driver's licence. Truck drivers' licences are downgraded following identification of medical problems. There are demerit point and licence-suspension programs as well as the enforcement of impaired driving laws and rules of the road. Three, vehicle safety enforcement. Vehicle inspection programs are carried out on company premises and on the roadside. Load security compliance is enforced by all but one province and the Territories and weight and dimension limits are enforced at all weigh scales. Four, insurance. All jurisdictions have mandatory insurance requirements. Five, dangerous goods legislation. This is very important for the transportation industry in Canada. Uniform laws and standards are in effect across the country covering vehicles, driver training and placarding.
On or before January 1, 1988, under the uniform code, the following eight new initiatives will be implemented in each and every province. First, the CCMTA single-driver licence concept is an upgrading of existing systems which will enhance enforcement and control. Second, the CCMTA classified driver-licence system will standardize the classification systems presently in place. Third, CCMTA medical standards for drivers will involve minor modifications to the present system. Fourth, CCMTA model regulations for security of loads will see minor modification to existing standards and participation by all jurisdictions. Fifth, training courses for dangerous-goods trainers is a new initiative designed to provide qualified instructors to teach drivers how to handle dangerous goods. Sixth, we will join the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance involving inspection and out-of-service criteria. Canada has a Canadian Vehicle Safety Alliance now in place which is similar, but all jurisdictions have agreed to join the U.S. Alliance for North American recognition and uniformity. This involves a roadside inspection system which is reciprocally recognized in each member jurisdiction. Seventh, individual companies had first-aid programs previously but now all but

February 9, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
drivers will be required to know first-aid to a national standard. Eighth, the carrier fitness, entry and control criteria complements the entry standards contained in Bill C-19.
I have just described a comprehensive set of minimum and uniform standards which will be in place before Bill C-19 is scheduled to be proclaimed on January 1, 1988, exactly as requested by the trucking industry and by Hon. Members opposite.
This is not all. There is more. The following 10 items will be implemented after January 1, 1988. By October 1988, vehicle maintenance standards will be uniform in all provinces. By January 1989, knowledge and performance tests for drivers will be uniform and standards will be raised. By January 1989, driver-examiner training programs will have uniform standards and will be expanded to provide ongoing training. By January 1989, hours-of-service regulations will be in place in all provinces and legislation for this is required in some provinces. By March 1989, self-certification standards and procedures for training drivers will be uniform in all jurisdictions. There will be two initiatives regarding records systems. By March 1989, operator profiles will be introduced. These will be safety records for each and every company holding a licence. By January 1989, driver profiles will be improved and the system will be made uniform in all provinces. By August
1989,	there will be procedures for the audit of employers' records. This new initiative includes a new enforcement procedure. By August 1989, there will be criteria for shortterm suspension of drivers' licences. This new initiative is designed especially for impaired drivers. By December 1989, the new enforcement of an interprovincial record exchange will be a tool which will give each province access to the profiles of all trucking companies and drivers. By December 1989, there will be a new enforcement measure for audit and inspection criteria which is aimed at compliance with safety requirements in terminals.
All of these improvements will be in effect before January 1,
1990,	a full year prior to implementation of the fitness-only entry test in Bill C-19. I also want to emphasize that the dates I have cited for full implementation mean that all provinces and Territories will be onstream by that date. Many provinces will have many of these items in place prior to those dates and some will even be ready with all elements before January 1, 1988.
This is a dynamic process. There will continue to be improvement to the system beyond 1990. It is completely unreasonable to ask that the safety code be completely in place before economic reform takes place. Some of the items I have mentioned require changes to provincial legislation and, therefore, cannot be proceeded with any faster. It is a red herring to suggest that we should delay economic regulatory reform until all the safety initiatives are in place. In many ways our safety system is far more advanced than that in place
in the U.S. As I said earlier, even there deregulation does not seem to have a measurably negative effect on safety.
In summary, it should now be apparent that, as the Minister of Transport has said on many occasions, safety of the transportation system is the number one priority. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brought in his economic statement in the fall of 1984, both opposition Parties predicted that hundreds of thousands of jobs would be lost.
My riding was under the thumb of the Liberal Government for almost 25 years. The rules and regulations of the transportation system under that administration did not work for us. There are three types of people in our society who depend entirely on the vast transportation system of our country. They are the consumers, the shippers and the carriers. The opposition Parties continually grandstand and make false predictions. They want to sow fear that things will not work. I can understand the mentality of the Liberal Party in saying that. For 25 years it made things not work.
Transportation is not a political issue. It is crucial to our society. We proved the Opposition wrong on the economy. We have reduced the national deficit while creating over 700,000 jobs. All regions of Canada have benefited. The Government does not believe in grandstanding and sowing fear in the hearts of Canadians. The Government believes in the consultative process and the economic development of the country.
In conclusion, I am honoured to be the vice-chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport to which Bill C-19 is to be referred. The fact that the Government is willing to refer this Bill to that committee and have public hearings shows the Government's openness and willingness to listen to concerned people. The Government wants a National Transportation Act which will allow our consumers, shippers and carriers to compete internationally.

Mr. Speaker, the issue we are dealing with here is as old as the country itself: is there any economic reason for Canada to exist? Bill C-18 and Bill C-19 have demonstrated the Government's tendency toward adopting the old laissez-faire economic philosophy that was popular at the time of American independence. The neo-conservatism of those in the current Reagan administration, which the Government of Canada is copying, has led to the philosophy of less government involvement in order to allow free market forces to prevail.
Unfortunately, if Canada indeed lets the free forces of the market proliferate, the market forces in this country will naturally switch from the east-west configuration that we have attempted to maintain since 1867 to a north-south configuration. When we compare our economies, our population, and the political and economic power that goes with their size, eventually the dominating force will come from the south.
We are not only talking about control of the trucking industry or its deregulation, as the Government attempts to say, but the economic future of Canadians. Indeed, will they have an economic future in Canada, where western Canadians and eastern Canadians continue to trade and provide the base on which social interaction can continue? Without social and economic interaction there will eventually be no political interaction. It is absolutely vital to the maintenance of this country that we keep those east-west links at work. The trucking system is only one of the many policies that this country has adopted over the years in an attempt to maintain Canada as a separate and independent nation.

Mr. Speaker, Alberta needs federal assistance, and it needs it now. There are over 30,000 people in my province out of work due to the drastic fall in oil prices.

Mr. Speaker, this past weekend First Choice Superchannel unscrambled their signal as part of a promotional exercise to increase subscriptions. As part of this sales gimmick, they continually suggested to viewers that movies appearing late at night could be taped on VCRs so that they could be enjoyed at a more convenient time. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to pay tribute to the Hon. Julien Chouinard, Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, who died last Friday. Mr. Justice Chouinard was well-known for his innate sense of justice and equity.

Born in Quebec City, he attended Laval University and Oxford University. He was a Rhodes Scholar and was called to the bar in the Province of Quebec in 1953. Mr. Justice Chouinard was Deputy Minister of Justice in Quebec from 1965 to 1968 and Secretary General of the Quebec Cabinet for seven years, and served Quebec as Judge of the Quebec Court
of Appeal for four years, truly a well loved son of Quebec. Mr. Chouinard was appointed to the Supreme Court of Canada in September, 1979.

He helped draft most of the judgments handed down by the Supreme Court and was a master of the written word.

Mr. Justice Chouinard's contribution to his province and country was great, and his loss will be felt by the legal community at large.

We mourn the loss of a judge who was truly exceptional. On behalf of the federal Government and of all Canadians, I would like to offer my sincere condolences to Mrs. Chouinard and her children.

subtopic: THE LATE MR. JUSTICE JULIEN CHOUINARD

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join my Opposition colleagues in paying tribute to the Hon. Julien Chouinard. I have a number of reasons for wishing to make my own contribution this afternoon. Personally, I had the privilege of working with Mr. Chouinard for several years, and Members on this side of the House have other reasons for mourning his loss. In fact, the Leader of our Party was a Rhodes scholar at the time Mr. Chouinard, also a Rhodes scholar, was going to Oxford. When Julien was President of the Junior Law Society of Quebec City, our Party leader was President of the Junior Law Society of Montreal. It is these memories that give us further reason to mourn the passing of a man who served this country so well.
As I said earlier, I worked with him when he was Secretary General of the Cabinet in Quebec City, and I and many Canadians with me are aware of the role he played during that very difficult time in October 1970.
Mr. Chouinard was, as they say in Quebec, "un homme solide", solid as a rock. He was level-headed, intelligent and a hard worker, but also very close to his family and a faithful friend. He had a sense of humour which he sometimes had trouble hiding behind a perpetually serious exterior.
When death comes as quickly as it did last Friday, it comes as a reminder to all of us in the midst of our busy lives that our existence is indeed fragile.
I wish to pay tribute to Mr. Justice Julien Chouinard, to his life and his career, and on my own behalf and on behalf of all my colleagues in the House of Commons, and of the Leader of our Party, I wish to extend to Mrs. Chouinard and all the members of her family our sincerest condolences.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise a point of order which arises out of your comments during Question Period with respect to the application of the sub judice convention. During Question Period, I understood you to say that the test of whether a question is consistent with the sub judice convention depends on whether it relates squarely to issues being litigated in a particular case. This is certainly an important test. I raise the point as to whether

February 9, 1987
Point of Order-Mr. H. Gray
there is another important test which I respectfully submit you should take into consideration in deciding whether the sub judice convention should be applied when deciding whether a question is acceptable when raised during Question Period.
Citation 335 on page 118 of Beauchesne's states:
Members are expected to refrain from discussing matters that are before the courts or tribunals which are courts of record. The purpose of this sub-judice convention is to protect the parties in a case awaiting or undergoing trial and persons who stand to be affected by the outcome of a judicial inquiry. It is a voluntary restraint imposed by the House upon itself in the interest of justice and fair play.
I point out in passing that this citation makes it very clear that the convention is there to protect the parties in a case, not other people who may have had some contact with the case either as witnesses, or who have some interest in the outcome, even if it amounts to nothing more than some curiosity about the matter.
I also might say in passing that there seems to be some conflict between citations with respect to the degree to which this convention applies to judicial inquiries.
Citation 338 states:
(1) Matters before a royal commission are not subject to the convention.
However, the main citation that I wish to bring to your attention in this regard is Citation 337, which is also on page 118 and it states:
(1)	No settled practice has been developed in relation to civil cases, as the
convention has been applied in some cases but not in others.
The citation further states:
(2)	In civil cases the convention does not apply until the matter has reached
the trial stage.
The source of this citation is House of Commons Debates, February 11, 1976, p. 10844.
As far as I am aware, and if I am wrong in this I am sure I will be corrected, the case involving Walter Wolf and Fred Doucet has not yet reached the trial stage.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: POINTS OF ORDER
subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF SUB JUDICE CONVENTION
speechtext: What is an examination for discovery?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: POINTS OF ORDER
subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF SUB JUDICE CONVENTION
speechtext:
Therefore, I submit that if the sub judice convention in the terms that you have stated it during Question Period is to apply at all, then it would come into play and is to be applied only once the case reaches the trial stage. I submit that an examination for discovery is not a trial. It is a proceeding before the trial, but it is not the trial.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask you to take into consideration the following submission. First, it is not clear that the sub judice convention, no matter how defined, is to be applied at all in any civil case, even at the trial stage. But if it is to be applied, including in the terms which you used during Question Period, then this application does not arise until the trial has actually begun.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully draw your attention to Citation 339 of Beauchesne's at page 119 in which the learned editor of this volume draws our attention to the report of the
Special Committee on the Rights and Immunities of Members which, among other things, recognizes that while "the Speaker should remain the final arbiter in the matter" of sub judice, he "should exercise his discretion only in exceptional cases. In doubtful cases he should rule in favour of debate and against the convention."
Because the matter with respect to the application of the sub judice convention will likely arise again in Question Period and in debate I thought I should take the liberty of making these comments for the purpose of saying first, the convention cannot apply to questions with regard to people who are not themselves parties or litigants in the case in question, and second, the the sub judice convention has not been clearly established to apply at any stage of a civil case, and third, if it should apply then it is only once the trial has begun, and it has certainly not begun in the case of Walter Wolf and Fred Doucet.
Finally, with the utmost respect, I draw your attention once again to what I suggest are the very wise words of the Special Committee on the Rights and Immunities of Members with regard to the degree of restraint a Speaker should exercise in applying the sub judice convention at any time.

subtopic: POINTS OF ORDER
subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF SUB JUDICE CONVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the arguments of my colleague, partly because I never did much litigation myself. I wish to make a couple of points. When reviewing this matter, Mr. Speaker, as I hope you will, it is in the interests of this House and Canadians who are before the court system at whatever level that you take due note of the words "in the interest of justice and fair play". That is what is at issue here when questions are asked.
There is another convention that was not contained in the argument of my hon. colleague, and that is as to what is the main purpose of Question Period. It has always been my understanding that the purpose of Question Period is for the Opposition to hold the Government accountable.
I submit that engaging in an examination of hearsay where an affidavit is filed, or evidence is taken by examination for discovery in which one individual in sworn testimony recounts what one person is purported to have said to another can hardly be referred to as hard evidence. When I went to law school it was hearsay. Whether it was sworn hearsay or not, it was still hearsay. The point here is whether we are putting at risk-I do not know why my colleague from the NDP finds the abuse of justice and fair play so funny. I do not.

subtopic: POINTS OF ORDER
subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF SUB JUDICE CONVENTION
speechtext: I was thinking of when you were in Opposition and some of the justice and fair play we used to see.

subtopic: POINTS OF ORDER
subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF SUB JUDICE CONVENTION
speechtext:
If my hon. colleague wants to argue the matter, let him. I suggest he do it. That is what this forum is for.
February 9, 1987

I think it is a very serious matter to interfere with the court process whether it is a criminal or a civil trial. I appreciate, as my hon. friend has pointed out, that the rules for civil litigation are not hard and fast, but fair play and justice are hard and fast. If for pure political purposes you are affecting the outcome of a criminal trial or a lawsuit in any way, shape or form, I do not think that is right and proper. I do not think my colleagues here want to indulge in that.
I would ask the Chair to look at that and I agree with my hon. colleague that it is something that should be looked at so there is some direction for the House as we go along. I urge that we zero in on the words "in the interests of justice and fair play" and decide whether or not this matter is being brought forward for purely political purposes or whether it is really holding the Government accountable. If that is the case, then I think we have to be sure that we are not tampering in any way with justice and fair play whether the litigant is a litigant in a civil matter or somebody being brought before the courts for criminal prosecution.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: POINTS OF ORDER
subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF SUB JUDICE CONVENTION
speechtext:
I want to thank the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) and the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lewis) for their contributions, and, I think it is appropriate to say, the Hon. Member for	Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). I think he deferred to the caveat the Chair put when he was asking a question and went to some pains to make sure that he did not transgress beyond the stage that the Chair felt it might not be appropriate to go. I want to re-emphasize that the Chair cannot always tell at the start of a question just exactly where that question may lead.
In specific answer to the point raised by the Hon. Member for Windsor West, I think there is something in what he says, that there may be some authorities which indicate a matter is not strictly speaking sub judice until it has reached the trial stage. There is some authority for that. That point was also brought to my attention in a note from the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. However, what I was hoping to do, and I am sure the Hon. Member for Windsor West knows this, was to alert members to the fact that there is a sub judice rule, and to ask members to be careful not to transgress against it. The Hon. Member for Windsor West and other Hon. Members will note that I have not ruled that a question has yet transcended that position, but I felt it was appropriate to make sure that everybody, as much as possible, understands the problem which the Chair has when these questions get increasingly close to that line.
The other thing I wanted to point out, and I think Hon. Members will agree, and that must also be understood, is that questions that are peripheral to the main issue being tested in the litigation are not necessarily excluded under the sub judice rule. It is important that all Hon. Members realize that, because sometimes there is a tendency for Members on one side to seize too quickly the conclusion that just because a
Point of Order-Mr. Lewis
question may concern some actors who may be involved in one way or the other in a lawsuit that it is by its very definition sub judice. I was trying to point out and draw Members' attention to the fact that that is not always so, and that the Chair has to find the middle ground.
I accept with great consideration the comments of the Hon. Member for Windsor West. I hope he will note that as this debate goes on and as these questions may go on that the Chair will try very hard to hew to what is the appropriate rule.
I think it is fair to comment that the point which the Parliamentary Secretary makes about the basis for this rule is that concern for justice and fair play must also be recognized in this Chamber. I must point out again that in all these matters, unless Members are cognizant of just those principles, justice and fair play, then sometimes that leads to a situation which may or may not create disorder, but may get very close to it, so the Chair sometimes has to try to move in very gently to keep that from happening. I thank the Hon. Member for Windsor West. The observations are cogent and they are helpful to the Chair.
The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary is rising on a different point of order?

Mr. Speaker, in response to the point of order raised by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader and President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lewis), I would note that one of the citations to which he refers, Citation 360(5), indicates that a question may not, as he pointed out:
reflect on the character or conduct of the Speaker or other occupants of the Chair, Members of either House of Parliament and members of the judiciary.
As the Hon. Member himself has acknowledged, these rules have to be read in light of the evolving practices and traditions of the House, and surely it is not reasonable to suggest that a member in Question Period may not ask a question which reflects on the conduct of a Minister of the Crown in the course of that Minister's activities vis-a-vis his or her government responsibilities. Surely to suggest that we cannot question the conduct of Ministers of the Crown is reading Beauchesne's Citation 360 in a manner which is not only out of date but which is completely unrealistic.
With respect to the suggestion of imputation of motives, I am not sure to what the Hon. Member is referring. In the initial question I asked, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) quite specifically to clarify the nature of his intervention in the telephone conversation in question and also to indicate whether or not there had been any suggestion of a withdrawal of a federal Government contract. In a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, I asked the Prime Minister again whether or not he agreed with the comments of his colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) that it was solely a private matter if, in fact, a Minister of the Crown intervened in a manner which had been suggested.
I suggest neither of those questions in any way imputed motives. They certainly asked about the involvement of the Prime Minister, but I suggest they are entirely within the framework and scope of Question Period and that if we cannot ask questions about the conduct of members of this Government, certainly that will significantly stifle an effective and free flow of questions during Question Period.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: QUESTIONS IMPUTING MOTIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I would like to make some brief comments on the point of order raised by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader (Mr. Lewis). The Parliamentary Secretary has admitted that Beauchesne's is not up to date and that the practice with respect to questions accepted by the Speaker during Question Period has certainly evolved, to use his word, since the edition of Beauchesne's in question was published. That is certainly accurate. The first citation to which he referred is from 1965, and no source is given at all for the second citation although this edition of Beauchesne's was published in 1978.
For some reason or other, the Government seems reluctant to draw attention to the guidelines for Question Period announced in the House less than two years ago by the previous occupant of the chair. Those guidelines may well have some bearing on this to the extent that you, Mr. Speaker, may wish to use them for guidance in the exercise of your discretion over which questions you will accept or not.
In any event, the citations from Beauchesne's about Question Period have not only been overtaken by a later set of guidelines set down by your predecessor but they have been overtaken by dozens if not hundreds of precedents established in this House day after day, week after week by questions asked by members of the Government when they were in opposition. Those questions were accepted by the Speaker without challenge or question and the questions were asked without doubt, shame or reticence of any kind. I say with the utmost sincerity and respect to you, Sir, that those are the precedents that cannot be overlooked in these circumstances.
Surely Beauchesne's Citation 360 cannot be interpreted literally as saying that the conduct of Members of the House who are Ministers cannot be questioned in so far as that conduct relates to their official duties. If that were to be the case, then Question Period as an essential element not only of the House of Commons but of the parliamentary system would be severely undermined and weakened. I would like to think that none of us would want to see that.
Finally, by way of authority, I would like to refer to the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader during the discussion on the point of order I raised just a few moments ago. He said that Question Period is to hold the Government to account. If that is the case, surely it must mean that one can question members of the Government about their conduct as Ministers. Second, if the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader is correct in saying that questions are not there to impute motives, he should not have said, as he did without challenge from me, that questions cannot be asked during Question Period if they are asked purely for-I think I recall his words correctly- political purposes. If that is not a form of imputing motives, what is?
In conclusion, therefore I think one must tread very carefully before saying that any questions which have some link with an inquiry into the purpose of the conduct in question are out of order because they impute motives. In any event, none of us should be ashamed about being willing to ask questions for political purposes. Is that not the reason for which we are here? We are talking about the operation of the political process which I hope will be exercised with the utmost integrity and trustworthiness. It is the political process that brings us here and it is the political process under which we are operating. Therefore, we should not be concerned if questions are asked for political purposes. I do not say that that necessarily imputes negative motives but I wish the Parliamentary
February 9, 1987

Secretary to the Government House Leader would be consistent in his arguments and would recognize that what he is complaining about has, as I said a moment ago, been well established by hundreds of precedents based on questions he and his colleagues asked when in opposition, questions which were readily accepted by your distinguished predecessors.

I would like to thank the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) and the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) for their interventions on this second point of order. The Chair is intrigued by the alleged suggestion that someone in this Chamber might be political. A distinguished former Member of this place is reputed to have said one evening in a moment, I think, of exasperation: "The trouble with this place is it's getting too political".
I think there will always be politics in a political forum like this one. When a suggestion is made that remarks are made for political purposes, I know that there are high political motives and there are perhaps less high political motives. It is for the Chair to decide to which of those two political motives the Hon. Member is referring.
On the question of the ancient or older precepts in some of the books that are sent to guide us, I think it has been made very clear that the Chair tries to take those rules or suggestions into account as a guide, but I think it is also clear to Hon. Members that the Chair has tried to temper those guidelines with the realities of the present situation in the House of Commons and the evolution of our procedures and customs. However, I do not think that anyone means that the conduct of Ministers or of Members, depending on what it is, is something with which the House cannot concern itself. What is key to this is that when questions are asked, Hon. Members should refrain as much as possible from using phrases or words that are accusatory or start off with an allegation relating to the character, honour or motives of any Hon. Member, whether those comments are made in a question or as a part of a reply.
Certainly vigorous and probing questions are completely in order in this place. I hope that I can persuade Hon. Members that I am very cognizant of the fact that that is part of our tradition. At the same time, I would say that the restraint, discipline and skill that is put into questions will probably elicit the information or put forward the position that is required without necessarily invoking a response which creates disorder in the Chamber and then creates a necessity for the Chair to intervene.
I thank all Hon. Members. As I say, we must look at these things as they come before us with a sense of fairness and justice and with a sense of what this place is all about. I think it will be a rare day when the Chair is too surprised that there is some politics in this Chamber.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just prior to the luncheon adjournment I was about to say that the Canadian trucking industry, for several reasons specific to its structure, will be particularly hard hit by deregulation.
Deregulation has had a devastating impact upon the American trucking industry-massive lay-offs, bankruptcy, increasing concentration, loss of service in the hinterland, et cetera. While that will be repeated in Canada, there is a very real likelihood that because of the particular character of the Canadian industry and the kind of geography with which it is faced, the consequences will be even more severe.
Three main features of the Canadian trucking industry must be borne in mind when we talk about the likely impact of deregulation-market size and orientation, what happens when we have a very large market alongside a relatively small one, and the present vulnerability of the Canadian trucking industry prior to deregulation. All these matters will have an impact upon the effect of deregulation in Canada.
Turning to market size and orientation, unlike the American market with its demographic concentrations, the Canadian market has only three large cities with populations of over one million people. While in the United States there are 1,722 city pairs with one million plus population, Canada only has six such pairings with a huge gap existing between Ontario-Quebec and the far west. Without regulation in the trucking industry in some form similar to what we have now, there will be little incentive to maintain east-west transportation routes and the historic basis of the country will be placed in jeopardy.
Present regulations with control over market entry, pricing, commodity, and destination restrictions have intentionally created a pattern of cross-subsidization of traffic through the encouragement of transportation generalists. For example, someone who wants to participate in the moving of less than fully loaded trucks applies for a licence, obtains a licence, services a particular area, and schedules his routes at well-known times. Thus, shippers and receivers of goods in those areas know when they will receive trucking services. In short,
3246

Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
the truck does not wait to be filled before making a run. The reduction or elimination of this regulatory control would encourage the super efficient and the transport specialists to the point of driving the transport generalist out of the market. Along with the demise of the transport generalist would come the demise of a great many small centres which are now providing goods and services to rural and lesser populated areas of Canada. With that goes the whole concept of maintaining east-west links in Canada.
The second aspect of Bill C-19 which I want to discuss, as it has an impact upon the trucking industry, is the size of the American market and our own market. When the United States introduced deregulation in its trucking industry in 1980, it did not have a large nearby neighbour with the geographic and economic capacity to enter and predominate in the transport industry. There was no nation 10 times or 11 times larger sitting just across the border to move in on its markets. With the upheaval caused by deregulation, the U.S. industry did not face the additional distraction of competition from an economically stronger and better prepared international competitor. However, Canada has that problem. We are faced with a neighbouring country which has been involved in deregulation for a number of years. It has consolidated its trucking business to the point where it has three very large companies which have almost taken over the market. It is in a position to treat the Canadian service market as a very small part of its market.
In fact, in the last six years one of the largest companies in the United States has expanded the terminals it services from 154 to some 540 or 550. It has indicated that it could serve most of the Canadian market in which it is interested by the establishment of another five or six terminals in Canada. One only has to look at highway maps of Canada and the United States to realize that that number would certainly be adequate for any U.S. trucking firm to service the most important aspects of the Canadian market. It could run through U.S. routes and take advantage of low cost fuel and low cost equipment. Our truckers estimate that the advantage of being based in the United States, paying U.S. licences, and buying U.S. fuel, amounts to about 10 per cent. That in itself is very difficult to overcome.
In addition, American companies have the advantage of being able to use the terminals they choose to set up in Canada as loss-leaders in order to get rid of existing competition in Canadian markets.
With more than 500 terminals one can readily see that a company, which only wants to expand its market by five or six terminals to get control of most of the Canadian market that might eventually be profitable, is not faced with any risk, even if it cuts prices by 50 per cent or as much as 65 per cent. Indeed, we have seen evidence where some of these companies have moved into new areas and have cut rates by as much as 65 per cent in order to get rid of existing competition and, immediately thereafter, switched to a form of billing more consistent with their pricing elsewhere in the country.
I have pointed out that the access of American companies to the Canadian market was relatively easy because they would only have to purchase a few terminals here. However, Canadian truckers do not have the same market advantage. They are operating in smaller markets and working from six to ten terminals scattered along the Canadian border. For them to penetrate the American market, five or six additional terminals would not do it. They would have to be prepared to expand by much more if they are to seize an important part of the American market, and the costs and risks would be simply too high. On the other hand, the penetration of the Canadian market is relatively easy for U.S. truckers, and Canadian truckers would find it difficult to compete.
The American trucking industry has been preparing for deregulation in Canada or for reregulation, as the Government prefers to call it, by analysing the market. It has also become involved in buying out trucking firms in Canada. A large trucking firm known as Yellow Freight System purchased three fairly substantial trucking companies operating out of the Windsor area in the past year. It now has a virtual stranglehold over that particular marketing operation. That industry has been preparing for deregulation in a way which will eventually make it pre-eminent in Canada as far as trucking is concerned.
As I said, the U.S. trucking industry is dominated by three very large firms-Yellow Freight System,Consolidated Freightways, and Roadway Express Incorporated. We are a little short of absolutely reliable figures about the structure of our trucking industry and its financial position, but available figures portray an industry marked by many small firms and a few very large firms, all of which are operating with a very slender margin of profit. The majority of the approximate 10,000 trucking firms listed in Canada are small operations with one to three trucks. Even among the very large trucking firms historically there has not been a pattern of large profits. An industry spokesman recently remarked that even in the best of times industry-wide profit levels seldom exceed 3 per cent. In 1984, 22 per cent of the companies reporting to the Ontario Trucking Association were suffering losses.
In 1985 there were at least four major takeovers and mergers which were precipitated by companies on the Canadian side attempting to get ready for the competition with which they will be faced from the U.S. side. Reimer Express Enterprises bought Inter-City Truck Lines in April to create one of the largest trucking companies in Canada. In August, Dominion Consolidated Truck Lines and Overland Express merged to create the largest trucking company in the Ontario region. That same month CP Express, Canada's largest road carrier, bought Pickard Moving and Storage. As well, Direct Transportation System was sold to Canadian Motorways, creating what The Globe and Mail referred to as the biggest shake-up in the industry so far.

All of these occurred within a few months of each other. I am sure that had we looked further we would have found even more concentration and mergers taking place. The same pattern emerged in the United States when trucking was deregulated there. I have already pointed out the extent to which that has happened with the domination by three very large firms.
One of the myths which accompanies deregulation is that with the elimination of government's visible hand competition will again be brought into the market. The theory is that the economy will revive, the consumer will again be sovereign, and there will be so many winners that the few losers will be grateful to be martyrs for the sake of efficiency. Indeed, that was the theory for a new world which the then Minister of Transport put forth when he presented his paper, Freedom to Move.
However, some of the trucking companies are less enthusiastic about this. In the U.S. less than 10 companies now control more than half of the industry's total profit. The irony of deregulation is that by opening the doors to unregulated competition concentration is promoted. This is the problem to which I have been alluding throughout my remarks.
One of the arguments which has been used by my colleagues with regard to the Government's efforts to deregulate is with regard to the road hazards which will be created. Even American truckers are admitting that regardless of safety provisions, deregulation brings hazardous road conditions. Carriers which operate on a shoe-string can hardly attend to matters of new tires or brakes overhauls when they live, as a vast majority of them will, from shipment to shipment. Trucking equipment will stay on the road longer as companies are forced to cut expenses for new investments to the bone. The quality of repair work and upgraded equipment will deteriorate in all but the most profitable of companies. Truckers, particularly small owner operator truckers, will drive longer stretches as they search for freight to ship, increasing the danger to themselves and to those with whom they share the highway.
That is what we are concerned about with regard to deregulation, or reregulation, whatever the Government chooses to call it. We think there should be a slow-down in the process to permit better understanding of what has happened in the United States and to give our industry an opportunity to make the necessary corrections to ensure that whatever changes occur in this country can be made with safety and security. We must maintain Canada with an east-west economy rather than a north-south one as this change of regulation tends to encourage.

Mr. Speaker, the member who just spoke and I both come from a resource based part of the country where thousands of men and women earn their living by producing products which are exported to other parts of the world, 80 per cent to the markets south of us. The member has repeatedly mentioned the trucking industry in which we on this side of the House have considerable interest, too.
Why do his remarks seem to pay no attention to the workers who create the goods which trucking companies move? Will he not bear in mind the number of people in his province and in mine who work on farms and in potash mines, and who produce pulp and paper, all of which create livelihoods for people in our provinces? I remind him that a number of shippers have been forced to establish trucking companies themselves because of the inadequate service trucking companies have provided under the status quo. That is something we are trying to deal with in this Bill. I would like him to comment on the men and women who work in the industries that create the goods to be shipped.
Is the member suggesting that the laws should be changed so that U.S. trucking companies in Canada that employ Canadians should be barred from Canada? If so, I point out to him that there are over 1,000 Canadian trucking companies in the United States doing business for Canada. He may not know that with virtually the stroke of a pen those 1,000 Canadian trucking companies in the United States could be expelled, which would be a loss to Canada.
I want the Hon, Member to speak particularly about the interests of those who produce the goods that are shipped by the trucking industry. Why did he not mention them in his speech?

Mr. Speaker, since I only had 20 minutes, I did not get to that part of my speech. It is my understanding from reading what happened in the United States that many of those companies, which believed it was in their best interests to provide their own trucking companies prior to deregulation, discovered they were forced to abandon those trucking firms because of the extreme competition to expand or maintain their market share after deregulation. Their routes were being invaded by some of the very large companies in an attempt to expand their market share.
For the short run it was actually more costly in many instances for manufacturing companies to use their own trucks to deliver goods because the competition was offering rates that were below the cost of production. I doubt this will continue for many years, but as long as some companies have control of a certain segment of the market, they can cut rates to much less than their real costs in the process of expanding simply to force out any competitors, including some manufacturing firms that had run their own trucking business.
I believe there is enough access to transportation services under our current system. I represent an area that is rather thinly populated and we appreciate the fact that there must be some effective cross-subsidization of the transportation system since there is not enough demand in the small villages and towns that I represent to warrant a full truckload of goods each week or more. We need some regulations requiring service so that heavy goods will be delivered when we need them. We are prepared to pay the higher price for that service.

I suggest that these Bills reflect the views of members of the Standing Committee on Transport as well as members of the previous Government and this Government.
It is nonsense to suggest that there has not been ample debate. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier is wrong. This Bill reflects the very spirit by which we hope this country can be revitalized, particularly in the transportation of goods. This Bill will provide shippers with the opportunity to compete in the shipment of goods. They will have the right to choose their method of shipping, obtain alternative tenders for shipping from various trucking companies and, according to Bill C-18, from other forms of shipping. It is a Bill designed to enhance the freedom to move. If we can make the freedom to move a real possibility, if we can get rid of the monopolies which have existed, the restrictions and curtailment on freedom of enterprise, then we can open the whole thing up and probably wind up with lower cost goods, more employment and better conditions for all.
I have a petition here from a company in Hinton, Alberta, with respect to the movement of its goods. It talks about the opportunity to move lumber and pulp to its American market by truck if it cannot make a deal with the railway. The company says the railways are effectively a monopoly and giving it the right to engage truckers, gives it the opportunity to break that monopoly. It is important that our various producers have the right to shop around.
Clause 22 of the Bill gives the definition of a public carrier, which is any railway company and any operator of an extraprovincial truck undertaking. Therefore, one of our largest agricultural products, grain, can now be moved by truck under the provisions of this Bill. I am surprised that this has not been recognized by the Opposition. I am surprised those Hon. Members would not realize that under the terms of this Bill, the system is being opened up. Some truckers are upset about this Bill, but they are established trucking companies which
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
have what we call in Ontario a public commercial vehicle licence or a PCV licence, which enables them to have certain monopolies on certain routes.
The theory behind this Bill is that the monopoly age is over. However, the New Democratic Party is today saying that it wants to support the continuation of the monopoly age. The Liberal Party says it wants to support the continuation of the monopoly age. How does that monopoly work? A particular trucking company has a monopoly, for example, with one kind of freight from one shipper to one point, or a Class A situation where it can ship goods of every nature and kind between two cities on a particular highway. The effect of that is to limit the number of people who can engage in shipping goods. When we limit the number of people who can do that, we have a monopoly. When we have a monopoly, those companies can get whatever kind of fare they want for the goods to be delivered, and can charge, generally speaking, what the traffic will bear. That kind of monopoly situation is what this Bill is designed to stop.
There are some problems. For example, a number of trucking companies have capitalized the value of their licences. The capital value of their licences represents a very important item on their balance sheet. They say to us that if we do away with these licences, they will lose the capital value of the licences. However, these licences are monopolies which allow those companies to operate their trucks in a protected fashion. Very much like a railway has a monopoly because it owns the track, they have a monopoly because they own the right to run certain freight down certain highways exclusively. If we want to continue with a society which believes in giving monopolies, then, obviously, the monopoly has a value.
One of the problems we face with this legislation is somehow phasing in the loss of that monopoly to the companies involved. The companies which have capitalized the monopoly in the normal fashion will be able, bit by bit, to write off their goodwill or the value of their licence which will get them the money back in the tax system. However, some companies have not capitalized their licences. They developed the licences a long time ago and they now have a real value but have never been capitalized. Those companies are going to have to accept that if a state gives a monopoly, a state has the right to take that monopoly away. Surely, in a free society, monopolies which have ceased to serve their purpose cease to have any right to be there.
I would have thought that the New Democratic Party would have recognized that monopolies in transportation should not exist. They should recognize that the borders should be open and those people who want to go into trucking should be able to do so as long as they have top-notch equipment and provide a good service. But the New Democratic Party wants to protect the existing situation. Those Hon. Members say: "Don't let it change", which almost defies the logic of a Party which would call itself new and democratic. It is supposed to be new and democratic yet is in favour of monopolies, in favour of the status quo and of ensuring that some people have

This House through this Bill throws the light on the situation. It throws open the situation. We are saying: "Look. If you want to get involved in interprovincial trucking, get yourselves some equipment and some local licences and away you go". That kind of freedom will make it possible for shippers to move their goods in a competitive fashion. We say that the greater good is the movement of goods. I say that, Sir, because one of the major problems we face in this country is the problem of regional disparity.
Earlier today the Mayor of Kamloops was in to see me. His Member of Parliament, the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis), arranged for him to come and see me with respect to a promotion by the City of Kamloops to attract business. The Mayor of Kamloops is a pretty optimistic fellow. He told me that Kamloops had an advantage by being on both the Yellowhead Highway and the highway which passes through Rogers Pass. It has the advantage of the two main Trans-Canada highways as well as the advantage of having both railways go through the town. He said: "We have these advantages and we want to make sure the people of Canada are aware of these advantages". The freedom of movement legislation, the right to be able to provide trucking any way one wants on an interprovincial basis, without the restrictions which did apply, ensures that cities like Kamloops will have a better chance at the business.
One of the problems has always been that the big cities attract the industry. Big cities attract activity because of the cost of shipping goods. If we are going to attack regional disparity, we have to attack the cost of shipping goods. We do not attack that cost by protecting monopolies and vested rights. This Bill is out to get rid of vested rights. It will allow people who want to go into business to do so on their own, to do it the way they want to do it. If we carry on with the present system we will continue to deprive the outreach parts of our nation of efficient cheap transportation.
It was said earlier by my friend from the New Democratic Party that somehow there is cross-subsidization involved. In trucking there is no such thing as cross-subsidization. If money cannot be made running a truck, then it is not run. That is the way it is. Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me the floor on this Bill which is very important for the whole country, particularly so for remote regions such as the Atlantic Provinces.
I feel somewhat restricted in taking part in this debate under present circumstances because the debate is limited. It is just like everything has been decided in advance and we are talking simply to kill some time. However, Mr. Speaker, I will proceed.
Needless to say, Bill C-19 respecting motor vehicle transport by extra-provincial undertakings is at the root of as much reaction and controversy as, and in certain cases even more concern than, Bill C-18, an Act respecting national transportation. Like C-18, this Bill as drafted opens the whole trucking industry to major changes and severe disruptions which might even be likened to an earthquake. This very severe disruption will shake up the industry and, if I still compare it with an earthquake, it will most certainly register between 8 and 9 on the Richter scale. The disruption will be so severe that long-established carriers will come crashing down. Its impact will be such that firms which have been in business for some time will become so weak that they will be easy prey for stronger and larger companies which will buy out or take over smaller concerns no longer able to operate in this new climate of deregulation.
Here we have an industry which is doing $8 billion worth of business and providing employment for over 50,000 people. Through Bill C-19 the industry will be sent on a mad race towards deregulation, which appears to be the answer to everything that ails us. Mr. Speaker, I do not want to imply that every single facet of deregulation is bad, but the way this Government is rushing into this process is alarming and leaves an element of doubt about the Bill.
The first major change brought about by this Bill has to do with the criterion concerning access to the industry, namely the existing public convenience and necessity criterion.
This requirement meant the carrier had to prove the proposed service was necessary and would be of benefit to the public. It will now be replaced by the requirement "fit, willing and able". This new requirement puts the onus of proving the service is not in the public interest on existing holders of trucking licences.
In future, anyone who has a truck and is "fit, willing and able" to go into business can get on the road. Mr. Speaker, your answer to that may be: More carriers will mean more competition and better service, so everybody should be happy. That is how it looks, but the situation contains an element of disaster that may severely affect Canada's industry, because, Mr. Speaker, our industry will be at the mercy of foreign carriers. This Bill will allow U.S. carriers to penetrate our market and take over a large part of the activity in this sector. This of course means less business for our Canadian carriers.
Mr. Speaker, I should add that our carriers will be placed in an entirely new situation with parameters that have nothing in

common with the present situation. If we compare Canada's transportation industry with the industry in the United States, we realize that our carriers will have to do battle with the giants, who in addition to the advantages of their size, which is considerable, will not hesitate to use any other means to take over our market. Anyone who is in the business is there to make money and make a profit, and in that case, the end justifies the means.
This Bill will now permit Americans to penetrate our market and to charge predatory rates. By predatory I mean rates below the going rate, rates that do not fully cover the service rendered. I would like to add, Mr. Speaker, that in a region such as New Brunswick, and especially southeastern New Brunswick, where a 17.1 per cent rate of unemployment was announced last Friday, such lay-offs are disastrous.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
