subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   IMMIGRATION ADVISABILITY OF REGULATING PRIVATE IMMIGRATION CONSULTANTS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   IMMIGRATION ADVISABILITY OF REGULATING PRIVATE IMMIGRATION CONSULTANTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to regulate private immigration consultants with a view to protecting unsuspecting prospective immigrants who seek advice from such consultants who are not subject to any codified regulations.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my Private Member's Motion deals with consumer rip-off by unscrupulous individuals who are running a cash-flow business on the backs of unsuspecting victims. The exploitation of potential immigrants by unscrupulous consultants has been going on, unchecked by any government action, for a number of years. It is getting worse; one can ask any Hon. Member.
A 1981 discussion paper outlined the problem and recommended courses of action. Unfortunately it was left to gather dust, although it contained many excellent ideas. The Department of Immigration has no comprehensive statistics on the number of immigration consultants operating in Canada, the type of service they provide, the fees they charge, or the incidents of misconduct. The Department has none of this information even though it was requested to obtain such in 1981 in a directive from the Minister. I have been told by senior officials of the RCMP that media reports suggesting large scale exploitation are not blown out of proportion and that exploitation by immigration consultants is widespread.
Recently I met with a constituent who was charged $10,000 by a consultant for writing two simple letters. Another prospective immigrant was charged $20,000 for filling out a social insurance application.
Unlike lawyers, immigration consultants are not subject to any regulations. They are not governed by a provincial law
February 9, 1987

society which can expel members for dishonest or exploitive conduct. This is the essence of the problem.
What control is there of immigration consultants? There is hardly any effective control because the Criminal Code does not deal with exploitive or dishonest conduct. It deals only with fraud in the extraction of fees. Almost always, transactions and advice between consultants and clients are oral and behind closed doors. These unscrupulous consultants are fully cognizant of the law and they know the parameters around which they can legally operate.
Prospective immigrants have a particular vulnerability. There is a tendency on the immigrant's part not to report an incident when one has been victimized for several reasons- first, a feeling of general distrust of government officials, perhaps based upon experience in the country of origin; second, the belief that to succeed in an application something more than mere compliance is necessary; third, a willingness to place special trust in an adviser simply because of a shared language or cultural background; and, fourth, simply to avoid making waves for fear of being viewed as a trouble-maker, thereby jeopardizing the potential success of an application.
Obviously not all immigration consultants exploit potential immigrants. Many provide a competent, useful, and necessary service. The discussion paper accurately pointed out that these consultants, more often than not, are the ones who appear before government boards and agencies such as the Immigration Appeal Board. In these cases criminal fraud is unlikely, and there is better opportunity for control by Government.
The present system is not adequate to deal with unscrupulous consultants. The federal Government has the responsibility to initiate legislation or some type of measure to make certain they are brought under control. In the discussion paper and in my conversations with departmental officials and with various ethnic communities, several courses of action have been suggested. Perhaps this type of activity could be left for the provinces to control under existing provincial legislation.
On the surface this may seem like a sufficient solution, but I hesitate to give it my concurrence. First, this is a national problem and I believe a clear national policy is required. Second, the law society has a very limited capacity for enforcement.
The issue of provincial government control brings up the question of the federal Government's constitutional authority to legislate in this field. I understand that the federal Government has jurisdiction to make regulations in the field of immigration consultants. Section 115(1) of the Immigration Act reads:
The Governor in Council may make regulations requiring any person, other than a person who is a member of the bar of any province, to make application for and obtain a licence from such authority as is prescribed before he may appear before an adjudicator or the board as counsel in exchange for any fee, reward or other form of remuneration whatever;-
The existing power would effectively control any immigration consultant appearing before a federal government board or agency. However, this is not the forum, as I stated earlier,
Immigration
in which unscrupulous consultants operate. The initiative would not go far enough.
Why not establish a federal registry for all immigration consultants operating in Canada, forcing all of them to be licensed. Standards would have to be met and heavy fines imposed for practising without a licence which, coupled with a greater effort by the Government to heighten the awareness within ethnic communities, would mean that all immigration consultants must be registered and must have a licence. We could achieve this buyer beware warning by diverting money already allotted to multicultural advertising.
Enforcement is essential to the success of such an initiative. The federal Government will have to instruct the RCMP to increase its investigation and monitoring activities. More emphasis will have to be placed upon the Enforcement Division within the Immigration Department.
Many caveats are associated with comprehensive licensing. Most obvious is whether the federal Government has constitutional authority. This question deserves serious thought and investigation by the standing committee.
Another concern is cost. How much would it cost to maintain a registry, issue licences, and have enforcement? The registry and licencing would cost nothing because it could be done on a cost recovery basis. Effective enforcement is another matter and it, too, deserves investigation by the committee. Equally important is the problem associated with immigration consultants operating in foreign countries.
In the few moments available to me I have outlined the problems associated with the proliferation of unscrupulous immigration consultants and have suggested a possible course of action. The problem is serious. It may not be in the headlines every day or on the minds of the majority of Canadians, but the activities of unscrupulous consultants are threatening the integrity of the entire immigration system, which will be hijacked by these pirates if something is not done.
If this type of exploitation were occurring on Bay Street or on the stock-market, government action would have been swift and decisive. Yet the problem continues and Governments, both federal and provincial, are silent. I urge that my motion be passed to allow it to be closely examined by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration so that effective recommendations for action can be presented to the Government.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   IMMIGRATION ADVISABILITY OF REGULATING PRIVATE IMMIGRATION CONSULTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me today to take part in this debate and to support my hon. friend's motion. I think we could discuss this matter for hours and not get anywhere by 6 p.m.

In the spirit of the new parliamentary system, I am pleased to say that, with an amendment, we should be discussing the matter in the appropriate committee. Indeed abuses are taking place and something must be done.

February 9, 1987
Immigration

For 25 years of my life, I have been involved with all these refugee issues. When I attended Ottawa University, I can remember as their president coordinating students' efforts in welcoming Hungarian refugees.
At the time, I was University President. Later, I became a Member of the House. I can remember during a visit to Vienna seeing all these people arriving from Czechoslovakia. Once more I had done my share either receiving them in Canada or helping groups willing to get involved in these matters. Later on, we could witness the integration of all those refugees into our Canadian society. I do not think that Canada has any lesson to receive from anybody when it comes to its generosity towards the so-called boat people.

We were away ahead of everyone in receiving these refugees. It is sad that people have the nerve to exploit those who are in the greatest need. They are being abused because they have nowhere to turn and no one to trust. The Hon. Member is absolutely right about that.
When the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) was the Minister responsible for immigration he initiated a major study on immigration consultants. We have a very major report on this question, which I am sure my hon. friend has seen and read. It is a discussion paper of April, 1981, entitled The Exploitation of Potential Immigrants by Unscrupulous Consultants. At that time we already knew that people were being exploited.
We would prefer to have a committee consider this motion rather than the Government in order that progress be made on the issue of exploitation. Way back in 1981 or 1982 the then Minister responsible for immigration initiated a number of steps including a special unit in the RCMP, special information programs, and special steps in the Department. I understand that the Department is, unfortunately, sometimes very reluctant to act in these matters.
In recent months my esteemed colleague and friend, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), has asked questions and given his support to the initiative which the Hon. Member has put forward today. I would be most surprised if members of the third Party in the House were not in agreement with us. I am sure we are all in agreement on the matter which is being put forth for our reflection today. However, it is not sufficient to reflect upon this matter; we want action.
Nothing has changed since the Minister made these studies. We thought that the creation of a special unit in the RCMP may send a message, but the exploiters of those who are in the greatest need still proceed.
Canada is still being built. We are building a little every day. I do not agree with people who say that Canada is an old
country. It is a young country which we are building every day. You are contributing in your own way, Mr. Speaker, as is the member who presented the motion. Each government tries to make an imprint. We need immigrants in this country. It is our duty to explain to Canadians that we need immigrants. It is our duty to explain to Canadians that in order to keep Canada as good as it is we need immigrants to ensure that there are enough workers in the country.
The so-called two founding races of this country-if I were an Eskimo or an Indian I would be very nervous to hear Prud'homme talking about the two founding races. Long before my ancestors came to Canada in the 1600s there were already people here. Therefore, I do not like the expression "two founding races". If there are two founding races, they are the Eskimos and the Indians. However, we know that the so-called two founding races, the Anglophones and the Francophones, are diminishing greatly. It is due to new immigrants that Canada is more prosperous and more populous.
Can you imagine what a bad image of Canada these immigrants have when they are exploited by unscrupulous consultants and unscrupulous lawyers? The time has come to study this issue attentively and determine what should be done. We need not study long because we have already done many studies, including those done by the Member for Winnipeg- Fort Garry in 1981, 1982, and 1983 when he was the Minister responsible.
In conclusion I will say that I am mainly in agreement with this motion, but believe I have to make an amendment. With the consent of my colleague who moved this motion and my esteemed colleague in the third Party, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), which shows very beautiful co-operation this afternoon:
That the motion be amended by deleting the words "in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of introducing" and replacing it with "the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration be empowered to study the advisability of the Government introducing",
I am honoured to present that amendment to Your Honour with the consent of the House. I thank the House for its good intentions.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   IMMIGRATION ADVISABILITY OF REGULATING PRIVATE IMMIGRATION CONSULTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to second the amendment moved by my friend, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), as well as to support the motion by the Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock). I believe that the proposal to empower the standing committee to look into the questions of unscrupulous immigration consultants and to work out means by which their activities can be regulated and hopefully eliminated is long overdue.
Let me note the comments which were made by the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North in his opening statement, as well as before the Committee on Private Members' Business when he appeared there. He stated in November that his staff had
February 9, 1987

spoken with the RCMP to get an idea of the scope of his problem. He said: "We were told that media reports suggesting large scale exploitation were not blown out of proportion. The RCMP claimed that exploitation by immigration consultations was widespread not only in Toronto but right across the country". That is how our federal police force views the problem.
It is deeply disturbing that despite the announcement by the then Minister of Employment and Immigration in 1981, under a former Liberal Government, he was asking the Department to get facts and figures on these abuses, about which many members have learned through dealing with our constituents, no such information has been collected by the Department in the last six or seven years. I believe it is an indication that the Department has failed to take this issue seriously.
I read the discussion paper in 1981. It became apparent that the Department does not want to accept the fact that there is a real problem. The options that were suggested by the former Minister became weaker and weaker as one read through the 1981 discussion paper. Finally, it sounded as though his officials were trying to persuade those who might read the discussion paper six years ago that there was really no problem.
However, as the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North indicates, the number of cases in which people are ripped off by unscrupulous consultants in this country and other countries where it is harder to investigate is legion. Immigrants as well as prospective immigrants are acutely vulnerable to this kind of exploitation.
One of the major activities in my riding office is to handle immigration cases. We attempt to give good and accurate information and we act as advocates, as I am sure do those in the offices of other members. Furthermore, this information and assistance is available for free.
While I do not recall any particular examples of overcharging by consultants, I know that the Immigration Department has put up road-blocks which have been extremely difficult to overcome. We have intervened on behalf of immigrants, sometimes successfully. However, it is clear that the pattern that has been developing is one in which the Immigration Department has been more difficult to deal with in recent years.
I suggest there are a couple of reasons for that. First, the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission has been consistently losing staff as a result of cut-backs by the previous and present Governments. People are short-staffed and working under stress, and their direction may be inadequate.
Second, the attitude of management within CEIC seems to have been that immigration officers should be trying to keep people out rather than helping them to get in. Immigration rules have been tightened, often without notice, making it more difficult for immigration. Consequently, if one does not have a particular angle to get into the country, one's chances of entry are quite limited.
Immigration
Many people want to come to Canada because they see it as a very fine country. They are prepared to accept the disadvantages of our climate and the 75-cent dollar when they compare our country to most other countries in the world.
The management in the Immigration Department still staffs heavily in Europe but lightly in areas like Latin America and Asia. Management seems to inculcate the attitude that such things as birth certificates and other documents in certain countries should not be recognized. There have been difficulties with legitimate refugees while others who claim refugee status may be more questionable but find it easier to get into Canada.
Finally, prospective immigrants feel vulnerable, fearing that they may ask the wrong question at the local immigration office. I might point out that when I discuss some cases with my staff I feel that we are vulnerable when acting for a prospective immigrant. We are very careful about how we frame our questions, for fear we may give the Immigration Department a piece of information that would allow them to turn down the immigrant. These are examples of problems which make immigrants vulnerable and encourage them to believe someone who promises them miracles for thousands of dollars.
I had an opportunity to read a letter written by the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) in response to a number of questions by our immigration critic, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), about the activities of immigration consultants. I fear that the attitude reflected by the management of that Department has changed little from 1981. There is a Panglossian optimism that is not justified by the facts.
The Minister states that he believes there are grounds for optimism. For example, he refers to a Private Member's Bill in Ontario, but we do not know whether the Bill will pass. Furthermore, as the Member for Etobicoke North pointed out, this is a matter for national action.
The Minister refers to the Department seeking a consensus from the Law Society and other groups with respect to licensing. Many consultants do not want a consensus so they can continue to be unregulated in the kind of rip-offs in which they are indulging right now.
I hope the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration provides leadership in this area. The Minister admits that despite efforts to get the RCMP to act, he cannot point to a lengthy list of successful prosecutions. He goes on to say that nevertheless, progress is being made and efforts are gaining momentum.
That is clearly not true. The Minister specifically indicates in his letter in January that early optimism about a register is now turning into rejection. This is another question that I believe the committee should study. I congratulate the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North, and while I do not agree with him on every issue, I suggest that he is certainly not only speaking on behalf of his constituents but also on behalf of his

Immigration
colleagues in all Parties. I hope Hon. Members will agree to allow this matter to go to committee before 6 p.m. tonight.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   IMMIGRATION ADVISABILITY OF REGULATING PRIVATE IMMIGRATION CONSULTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate this afternoon on Motion No. 45, presented by the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock).
Mr. Speaker, to help Canadians understand this afternoon's debate, I think it might be useful to repeat the contents of Motion No. 45 for their benefit.
The motion says:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to regulate private immigration consultants with a view to protecting unsuspecting prospective immigrants who seek advice from such consultants who are not subject to any codified regulations.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) has proposed an amendment to have this motion referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, for further consideration.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to clarify the scope of this motion, because there are certain people, certain advisers, who take advantage of the naivete of immigrants who want to enter Canada.
Where this motion refers to consultants, these are people other than lawyers who, for a fee, give advice or represent their clients in immigration cases. I may remind the House that many immigration consultants are competent people and do useful work by providing pertinent advice that is of benefit to their clients. However, since consultants do not have to observe certain standards regarding conduct, fee schedules and knowledge of Immigration legislation and programs, the result has been to attract a certain class of unscrupulous individuals who pass themselves off as immigration consultants.
Mr. Speaker, the 1981 report of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, gives a number of examples. For instance, two sisters had to pay a fee of $14,000 to a consultant who promised to get their sister back to Canada. Fourteen thousand dollars is a lot of money! There were other examples. One consultant demanded $1,000 for representing a foreign national before the Immigration Appeal Board, although his services were of no use to his client. Some people had to spend $1,000 to obtain what turned out to be shockingly little information on how to claim refugee status.
Mr. Speaker, there is a certain degree of vulnerability among immigrants, and it is this kind of abuse that must be dealt with.
Some people are vulnerable because, generally speaking, they are suspicious of public servants and have more confidence in a consultant who speaks the same language or has the same culture as themselves, and they believe that such a consultant can give them a certain advantage. Immigrants to Canada are not suspicious enough, and this leads to abuses.
Very often, such consultants operate openly in Canada or abroad. In Canada, their services range from giving simple advice to representing their clients at hearings or before the Immigration Appeal Board in accordance with the Immigration Act. As an example, we have seen the recent inflow of Turkish citizens claiming refugee status, who had been advised by foreign consultants. As Canada supports immigration, some consultants will have other opportunities to abuse the situation unless our Government attacks this problem.
One possible solution would be to include in the Immigration Act provisions to deliver licences to consultants and regulate their activities. Potential immigrants would tend to go to certified consultants and unauthorized consultants could be sued. However, legislative action does have certain drawbacks. Among other things, we would need to create a mechanism to apply the regulations. This would be one method to deal with the very real problem of unscrupulous consultants who give their foreign victims a very bad image of Canada.
Other recourses are available to immigrants. Of course, they could institute proceedings under a provincial consumer protection legislation or obtain better immigration services. However, court proceedings could create various problems for immigrants.
It is difficult to put together a strong case when clients refuse to testify.
On the other hand, we cannot institute proceedings against consultants operating in a foreign land. There could also be an attempt at solving the problem by increasing the quality of our immigration services to such an extent that seeking advice from a consultant would become an exercise in futility. Among other things, we could make information more readily accessible, increase the availability of staff for consultation purposes, keep NGOs better informed and encourage their participation.
For the time being, people continue to seek advice from consultants; many of them are competent and honest. However, others are taking advantage of their customers. We should also consider the advisability of introducing legislation to regulate private immigration consultants as a means to remedy this situation.
Mr. Speaker, I should like therefore to support motion No 45 moved by our colleague the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock), as well as the amendment just moved by the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme). I indicate my support and wish regulations be enacted to restrain the activities of immigration consultants.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   IMMIGRATION ADVISABILITY OF REGULATING PRIVATE IMMIGRATION CONSULTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased today to rise to support this motion. I am particularly pleased given the fact that this motion has received the support of both the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party. I hope that through
February 9, 1987

actions such as this we can get the equilibrium of the House re-established.
One of the focuses of the debate this week has been ethics, so perhaps I can start off by saying I have a direct conflict of interest with respect to this motion. I have the largest, most populous riding in the country. Something like 60 per cent of my constituency work has to do with immigration. A very good proportion of that 60 per cent has to do with the unscrupulous dealings of immigration consultants. I am very determined to reduce my work-load by seeing this motion passed so that we can put these people out of business.
I want to stress, of course, that there are many competent immigration consultants who provide accurate and helpful advice to their clients. Such consultants make beneficial contributions to the immigration process. My problem is that I hear about these people but do not get to see them. The cases which are handled successfully by these consultants do not end up on my desk.
It is obvious that we have a large number of individuals other than lawyers who purport to be immigration consultants. They enter the field untested as to their knowledge of immigration, with no form of qualifications, and charge fees they themselves set which are beyond those of any sort of professional regulatory body. These fees are not trivial. Sometimes they are in the thousands of dollars. There have been cases where fees are charged into the tens of thousands of dollars.
These so-called immigration consultants offer advice to people, in some cases, which is completely impossible to fulfil. Case after case has come into my office where people have been taken by these so-called immigration consultants for every penny they have, and only when they run out of money does the consultant suggest they see their Member of Parliament to see if he can straighten out the problem.
I have a very direct interest in seeing this motion passed today. Mention was made of the earlier 1981 discussion paper on unscrupulous immigration consultants. I believe it is time to take direct action. I congratulate the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock) for bringing this motion forward because I believe those of us from areas where there is a very heavy immigrant settlement are determined that these unscrupulous practices be condemned and stopped.
Not only do these practices take place in Canada but they also take place abroad. People come to me and tell me they are paying large amounts of money to so-called consultants, often Canadians, who operate abroad in cities such as Hong Kong. They hold out a promise that they have an inside track to our embassies and can get these cases through. As we all know, they do not have these inside tracks. What they do have is the ability to gouge people of large amounts of money and then, after they have taken their money, they just throw them aside.
I want to see the motion passed today. In conclusion, I think that the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock)
Immigration
should be congratulated by the whole House for bringing this motion forward. I hope to see us vote to accept both the motion and the amendment so that speedy action can be taken on this matter.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   IMMIGRATION ADVISABILITY OF REGULATING PRIVATE IMMIGRATION CONSULTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate, especially since I have the impression this is a Private Member's motion that has a chance of being adopted. There is a chance it will get things done. That is important. The motion presented by the Hon. Member in the House today concerns a very important matter. It is about immigration consultants. I think all members will agree there is some exploitation going on in this area and that it should stop.
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to see all Parties expressing the same views and taking the same perspective on a matter of this importance. Previous speakers have testified to the realities of this problem. I know from my own experience that it is a very real problem. Hon. Members have indicated that a report by the RCMP mentioned the problem existed across the country.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to point out that so far, the Department of Employment and Immigration has neglected to collect a body of information on the subject. Because of this, I think it is very important that this House should point out the urgency of the matter and indicate to the Department that the question must be given consideration. I think individual members should point out to the Government that all of us as members of all three Parties want to see some action in this area.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the very existence of these consultants who exploit immigrants indicates a need for information on immigration regulations, information that should be more readily available, not just outside the country but also within our borders. Many of my constituents, many residents do not know all these immigration regulations. There is a real need for information here.
Mr. Speaker, I also want to say that nearly all immigrants in my riding are concerned over the question of family reunions. Immigrants who are in Canada want their relatives in other countries to join them here, and this is indeed a very strong incentive. Everybody can appreciate that. All Canadians can readily understand that immigrants want their relatives to be with them here in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I think that because of such a strong incentive those people can easily be exploited by individuals who are not really interested in the plight of immigrants.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would simply point out that if we want to implement a fair immigration policy, if we want to open our doors to immigrants and protect them from people who exploit their situation, we must have a full employment policy in this country because the more Canadians we have on the unemployment lists the stronger the political pressure to stem the flow of immigrants. This creates a climate such that immigrants find it very difficult to come to Canada, and those
February 9, 1987

Immigration
who are already here are thwarted in their efforts to have their relatives join them.
In a nutshell, Mr. Speaker, we cannot expect to have a more equitable immigration policy unless we first begin by advocating a full employment policy.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude my remarks by commending my colleague for introducing this motion in the House, a motion which calls for action.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   IMMIGRATION ADVISABILITY OF REGULATING PRIVATE IMMIGRATION CONSULTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy indeed to second the motion of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock). I welcome this opportunity to speak on the matter of unscrupulous immigration consultants. Although they represent a small minority, their actions nevertheless threaten to disrupt the entire immigration process. Not only do they make a mockery of the system and the essential work done by their ethical colleagues, they prey upon prospective immigrants in a merciless fashion. I have seen this happen in my riding of Willowdale.
Immigration clients are, unfortunately, vulnerable for all the various reasons mentioned by my colleague. In desperation and ignorance they often turn to these charlatans as their best hope for obtaining immigrant status. The results for the unsuspecting client can be very serious indeed.
One odious aspect of this exploitation is the cost involved. The victims are powerless and often poor. The fees charged by these unscrupulous consultants are large, sometimes SI0,000 and more. Once the fee has been paid, the victim has no recourse under the law if the consultant wilfully fails to provide a service. Many prospective immigrants in my riding do not know that their MP provides this service for free and that he wants to see family reunifications happen as quickly as possible.
While the situation is obviously intolerable, we must nevertheless appreciate that the majority of consultants provide a valuable service. Therefore, we are pursuing several avenues to rid the system of the impostors and to protect potential immigrants from exploitation. The Hon. Member for Etobicoke North is proposing new legislation, but there are other options to be considered as well.
First, the CEIC Immigration Group maintains an active, ongoing dialogue on legal issues and immigration practices and procedures with the legal community. It shares our concern for the increased numbers of unregulated and unscrupulous consultants and is equally anxious to put a stop to them. Out of these discussions have come three principal recommendations that merit serious consideration. Alas, they have inherent problems as well.
To begin with, there is a suggestion that licensing would be an economical and effective method of control. It would seem to be the logical solution, but I can see a couple of complications. Who would be responsible for the licensing? Might not the licence itself become a licence to continue these unscrupulous practices? Certainly, the commission could not take on this role because of the impossibility of being open to accusations of conflict of interest.
The second proposal concerns requiring independent immigration consultants to work for and under the supervision of lawyers. That is a possible solution, but it narrows the definition of "counsel" under the Act to mean legal counsel. Therefore, it restricts the clients' right to counsel. We must not forget that many clients still prefer to have their clergyman, community leader, or other concerned individual present their case at a hearing.
The third major recommendation deals with the importance of educating the public, both here and outside Canada, about proper immigration procedures. The commission recognizes this need and it has increased its public relation campaign to inform prospective immigrants that free counselling is available at all Canadian immigration centres.
Finally, I wish to address my colleague, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North, and the recommendation that we amend the present legislation or propose new legislation to regulate private immigration consultants. Awarding licences to or regulating a professional group would normally be a provincial matter and not federal, particularly if members of that group are appearing before a federal appeal board. For either level of government in a time of fiscal and manpower restraint the cost of a regulatory bureaucracy is an important consideration. As well, there are hurdles in enforcing more stringent legislation. The RCMP has no jurisdiction to investigate the many cases which arise outside of Canada. The activities of these unscrupulous consultants are often, strictly speaking, not illegal.
I hope that it is apparent to all present that any new legislation would be one of many options, all of which bear important implications. We are all committed to ridding the system of these impostors. The real victims of their unscrupulous behaviour are the immigrants.
I fully endorse my colleague's motion, as well as the amendment made by my hon. colleague for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme). I trust that this evening we will be able to come to a vote and send it to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Kilgour (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   IMMIGRATION ADVISABILITY OF REGULATING PRIVATE IMMIGRATION CONSULTANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also am delighted to speak in this debate. If I may paraphrase, the motion and the amendment together basically state that all Parties in this House wish the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration to consider legislation to regulate private immigration
February 9, 1987

consultants with a view to protecting unsuspecting prospective immigrants who seek advice, and so on.
I wish to speak in favour of both the motion and the amendment. Very briefly, I should declare my conflict of interest, as did my colleague, the Member for York- Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan). His riding has about 270,000 people, and my riding has about 120,000. In York-Scarbor-ough about 54 per cent of the people in that constituency have a first language which is not English. Edmonton-Strathcona has about 62 per cent of the people in that constituency who originate from other than France or Britain. Not all are first generation, but a large number are.
I wish to start by making the point that in my view immigration creates jobs, it does not take them away. I am reminded that in York-Scarborough the unemployment rate is now 3 per cent or under. Mississauga also has an unemployment rate of 3 per cent or under. These two areas presently have the highest rates of immigration, and they are the areas in the country which have the lowest unemployment rate.
It seems to me that the point is clear from all objective evidence that newcomers create jobs rather than take them away. As you will recall, that was the experience of Edmonton in its period of boom. The more people that came, the more jobs that were created, the lower the unemployment rate. That is why we are increasing the level of immigration in Canada. We know that immigrants create jobs for services, houses, schools, and all the things that create a healthy economy. They also reinforce the multicultural nature of Canada. Immigration and multiculturalism represent the solution to many of Canada's problems, they do not represent problems to Canada. The independent class of newcomers will be targeted at 48,000 to 55,000, including dependants. I am pleased that the target is increasing this year, and it will increase in the future.
The Government believes in immigration and the arrival of newcomers to Canada. Our birth rate is now between 1.4 and 1.6 per cent. It becomes clear that unless something is done about the birth rate, it will only be a large number of newcomers which will allow us to pay the pensions for the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) and the Hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan), or any of the other members or people in this country.
I wish to say that I strongly support the motion. There are many ethical immigration counsellors in Canada, but there are also some unethical ones. We are all trying here today, in a great show of non-partisanship, to get at the unscrupulous ones, whose practices are widely condemned. It is particularly regrettable that these people ply their trade with people who are often vulnerable because of language, or because of economic problems as newcomers, or because of family concern about officials from other countries. Mr. Speaker, you know what the consultants did in Turkey or Portugal. Unfortunately, they have done things outside of Canada which have affected the attitude of many Canadians toward newcomers. We all regret that, which is doubtless one of the reasons we are doing this today.
Adjournment Debate
An obvious way to control unscrupulous consultants is to provide immigration services so easily and so comprehensively that clients will not think that they have to get a consultant. In Edmonton there have been problems with line-ups, and on occasion problems with people being mistreated. There are many immigration officers in Edmonton who are excellent people. They are sympathetic and they understand the tension that the people are under. We wish to make services more accessible.
I would move, Sir, that the question now be put.
